I’m Tripti, growing up in Delhi made me curious about people, public spaces, and the stories unfolding around me every day. Design became a way for me to explore those questions and better understand the world around me.

I’m especially interested in new media and immersive experiences. I work across interfaces, 3D environments, physical computing, and print, exploring how different mediums shape the way an experience is felt.

Outside of design, you’ll usually find me reading, watching films, or cooking. They keep me grounded and continually introduce me to new perspectives and ways of thinking. By day I’m a designer, and by night I am…

Remnant

Remnant is a video poem that reflects on the way humans experience time.

Overview

Remnant is a video poem that reflects on the way humans experience time. It explores memory, emotion, and the moments that shape us, suggesting that time is both a human construct and a force beyond our control. Through fragments of everyday life, it reveals how we become remnants of what we remember.

Taarghar (तारघर)

The Telegraph Office — a group installation, Semester 6

A user translating bodily gestures into rhythm, signal, and print — turning the body itself into part of the telegraph system.

Overview

Taarghar is a group installation built for a Multi Sensory Design studio, with Simran, Pranjal, Priyanka, and me. We recreated a telegraph office as a physical space—real desks, a tiffin, paper forms, a telegraph key—paired with a screen that reacts to what a visitor does with their hands. Opening the tiffin, filling the form, tapping the key, or performing a sign-language gesture each triggers the screen in real time through Morse sound signals and printed telegram outputs. The visitor's hands stay in the real world; the screen extends that world into the operator's office.

Context

The Indian telegraph service shut down in 2013, ending 160 years of a system that once carried the country’s most urgent news. An entire sensory world disappeared with it: the tap of keys, the sound of a morse key, the feel of writing on forms, the weight and smell of a tiffin on a clerk’s desk. We wanted visitors to feel what it was like to be inside that office rather than just look at it. A real telegraph office worked through the senses—writing, stamping, tapping, touch, smell, gesture—so the only honest way to bring it back was to let the visitor do those things themselves.

My Part — Signs and Signals

My interaction within the installation, Interaction 5: Signs and Signals, reimagines Morse code through the body instead of a mechanical key. Before digital communication, telegraph operators transmitted messages through rhythm, timing, and coded pulses. This interaction lets a participant communicate the same way through sign-language gestures: the system recognizes the gesture and translates it into Morse code sound signals and a printed telegram output, turning communication into a physical process of movement, rhythm, transmission, and documentation.

Rather than watching communication happen on a screen, the visitor experiences it through their own body—a way of reflecting on accessibility, mediation, and alternative forms of communication.

How It Works
1

Enter the office

The user enters the telegraph office installation.

2

Read the chart

They observe a sign-language chart showing the recognizable gestures.

3

Perform the gesture

The user performs the gesture in front of a webcam.

4

Recognition

A Teachable Machine model detects and classifies the gesture.

5

Translate to Morse

TouchDesigner converts the recognized gesture into Morse code and telegraph-like sound pulses.

6

Print the telegram

A thermal printer outputs the translated message as a printed telegram slip.

7

Feedback

The user receives visual, auditory, and physical confirmation all at once.

Build

The pipeline ran on a webcam feeding a Teachable Machine model for gesture recognition, with TouchDesigner handling the translation into Morse code and audio, and a thermal printer producing the physical telegram slip. Building it meant training the gesture-recognition model in Teachable Machine, wiring the Morse-code-and-sound logic in TouchDesigner, and getting the thermal printer to auto-print cleanly on cue.

Reflection

What Worked

Real-time gesture recognition successfully translated sign language into Morse code. Morse audio feedback made the transmission process easy to follow, and the thermal printer gave the interaction a physical, tangible output. The workflow from recognition to print felt immediate and responsive.

What Didn’t

Some gestures were misclassified under inconsistent lighting or hand positioning, and detection accuracy dropped when gestures were performed too quickly. A limited gesture dataset also restricted how many signs the system could recognize.

Limitations

The system currently supports only a set of selected gestures or letters rather than full sentences, and it needs controlled camera framing and lighting to stay reliable.

Credits

A group project for Multi Sensory Design, Semester 6, with Simran, Pranjal, Priyanka, and me. My contribution was Interaction 5 — Signs and Signals, the sign-language-to-Morse-code system described above.

AlignR

context.

Our physical computing module asked us to pick an everyday problem and build something that works. We kept coming back to how we sit. After hours at a desk, slouching becomes the default, and nobody notices the moment it starts.

the problem.

About 64% of employees sit for more than nine hours a day. You start upright, lean in to read something, and stay there. Over time that leads to muscle imbalances, stiffness and back pain.

the challenge.

How might we encourage better sitting posture for desk-bound workers so that they avoid long-term back issues?

who it's for.
mainly
desk-bound workersoffice workersstudents
also
elderly peoplegamers
insight.

Slouching starts in the upper back.

Most slouching begins around the T6–T8 vertebrae, the middle of the thoracic spine. That gave us a stable spot for the sensor, right where the slouch begins.

explorations.

We tried two ways of keeping the sensor on the body before landing on the third.

01 / tried

Neckband

Rested around the neck, close to the upper spine.

× neck discomfort× shifts as you move

02 / tried

Strap-on belt

A padded module held in place with shoulder straps. Stable, but slow to put on.

× bulky× restricts movement

03 / final

Adhesive patch

A small patch that sticks to the upper back with silicone adhesive. Nothing to strap on.

✓ light and discreet✓ easy to apply
form exploration.

We sculpted shapes by hand to find something that sits comfortably against the back, then took the strongest ones into 3D. Click any image to see it larger.

digital renders

outcome.

AlignR is a small patch worn on the upper back. It tracks the tilt of your spine, notices when a slouch lasts more than 10 seconds, and nudges you to sit up. No screen, no app.

circuit.

The first working prototype. Tap a part of the circuit to see what it does.

Powered by a 9V battery.

how it works.

Inside is a motion sensor that reads the tilt of your upper back. Try it: drag the person (or the slider) forward to slouch, and hold it there.

bzz

Sitting upright. Drag forward to slouch.

  1. 1

    Track the lean

    The sensor on the upper back reads how far you tip forward.

  2. 2

    Cross the line

    Leaning in for a moment is normal. Nothing happens until you pass the slouch line.

  3. 3

    Wait before reacting

    The ring fills while you stay slouched. The real device waits 10 seconds; this demo waits 4.

  4. 4

    A gentle nudge

    AlignR buzzes until you sit back up.

3D World BuildingVRUnity

Mautam
The Famine

Mautam is an immersive VR experience set in the bamboo forests of Mizoram in 1862, just before the flowering of Melocanna baccifera.

Overview

Mautam is an immersive VR experience set in the bamboo forests of Mizoram in 1862, just before the flowering of Melocanna baccifera. This rare ecological event occurs once every 48–50 years, producing an abundance of bamboo seeds that trigger rat population explosions and eventually lead to widespread crop destruction and famine.

The Experience

The user takes on the role of a colonial botanist commissioned to collect specimens of Melocanna baccifera for the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. Through interactions such as harvesting bamboo, preserving it in a Wardian case, and reading field notes, the player experiences the routine of nineteenth-century botanical exploration.

Design Intent

Rather than recreating a historical event as a spectacle, Mautam uses VR to immerse players in the material routines of colonial botanical exploration. Through physical interaction and environmental storytelling, the project invites reflection on ecology, extraction, and the unequal histories that shape how natural phenomena are remembered.

Key Interactions
  • Explore the Forest — Experience the bamboo landscape before masting.
  • Harvest Bamboo — Use a machete to cut a bamboo shoot.
  • Use the Wardian Case — Store the specimen for transport.
  • Read the Journal — Uncover the botanist's observations.

Why These Interactions?

These interactions recreate the routine of a colonial botanist, allowing players to experience the process of botanical collection while reflecting on the relationship between scientific exploration and ecological history.

Blender Assets

Environment and prop assets were modelled and textured in Blender — from the botanist's hut to the machete and field journal.

Unity Environment

The assets were assembled into a playable VR scene in Unity — a dense bamboo forest, the botanist's hut interior, and the wider landscape the player explores.

VR Walkthrough
Contribution

Research  •  Narrative Design  •  Interaction Design  •  Unity Development  •  3D Asset Modelling (Blender)

Data VisualizationGraphic Design2026

365 Days,
365 AQI Levels

For elderly people in Ahmedabad, air pollution isn’t a number — it’s coughing, fatigue, and breathlessness.

Overview

For elderly people in Ahmedabad, air pollution isn't a number — it's coughing, fatigue, and breathlessness. This project translates AQI into a familiar wall-calendar, using colour and body-based cues instead of apps or dashboards.

It turns AQI into a slow, everyday reminder that links pollution to symptoms and safer daily choices.

Target Audience
Age60+
LocationAhmedabad
Living ConditionsLower-middle-class urban homes, usually without air purifiers or sealed interiors.
Current StateSymptoms like coughing and fatigue are dismissed as ageing, not linked to daily AQI.
Why ThemOlder adults are most vulnerable, yet most AQI tools assume digital literacy. The calendar fits their existing routine.
Data & Methodology

CPCB AQI Data

Five years of CPCB AQI data for Ahmedabad revealed seasonal patterns and year-to-year shifts.

WHO Health Reference

WHO guidelines helped translate AQI numbers into body-level health cues for vulnerable, older bodies.

Growth-Based 2026 Projection

A simple growth-based projection estimates 2026 AQI from past trends.

  1. Step 1 Find the historical average AQIavg = average AQI from 2021–2025
  2. Step 2 Measure total change % growth = ((AQI2025 − AQI2021) / AQI2021) × 100
  3. Step 3 Convert to yearly growth Yearly growth = % growth / 4
  4. Step 4 Estimate 2026 AQI AQI2026 = AQI2025 × (1 + yearly growth)

This projection is used as a design estimation method, not as a scientific forecast.

Design Intent

Mental Shift

To move air pollution from an invisible background condition to a daily, body-level reality.

Micro-Decisions

To help elderly users decide when to walk, when to shut windows, when to avoid outdoor activity, and what symptoms to discuss with doctors.

Accessibility

To make AQI understandable without depending on apps, dashboards, or high data literacy.

Final Output

A physical wall calendar that turns AQI from numbers into a daily body-health guide. Each day's colour, plus pollutant and health cues, links pollution to real symptoms and safety actions.

It works as both an information object and a daily reminder — bringing environmental data into the home in a familiar, low-tech format.

How to Read the Calendar

Each date = one day of AQI data

Colour = air quality risk level

Light yellow — lower risk
Orange — moderate risk
Dark orange / red — high risk

Clusters of dark days = repeated exposure

Use the calendar to decide when to:

  • Go out
  • Reduce outdoor activity
  • Close windows
  • Wear a mask
  • Watch for symptoms

Thela,Thaila,ThikanaMunicipal Market, Ahmedabad

tl;dr.

we studied

How vendors, shoppers and workers in one of Ahmedabad's oldest markets cooperate, clash and adapt.

we found

People aren't against change. They're afraid of losing their place in it.

we made

A zine you can hear, smell and touch, carrying the market's voices and routines.

the market.

Municipal Market, "MM" to most people, sits next to C.G. Road, one of Ahmedabad's busiest streets. It opened in the 1970s and was one of the first hangout spots in the western city through the 1980s. Shops ring a central courtyard that doubles as parking, and the western entrance fills up with food stalls.

tap a part of the plan

Shops on three sides, parking in the middle, food at the western entrance.

Schematic, not to scale.

  • opened in the 1970s
  • ~7,000 m² in all
  • 49 small shops
  • ₹75–750 original monthly rent, set by the AMC
who's there.

The people selling here range from kids of 7 or 8 to people in their 60s and 70s. Some have worked here for decades; many food-stall workers have come from much further away.

7age of sellers70+

where they come from

AhmedabadRajasthanBiharUttar PradeshNepal

Migrant communities are especially present among food-stall operators and support staff.

economic background

  • manyeconomically disadvantaged, relying on vending as their main income
  • somelower-middle class, with steadier income
  • a fewmiddle class, with established or specialised businesses
research question.

What drives the cooperation and conflict among different stakeholders in Municipal Market, and how does it shape their openness or resistance to change?

how we listened.

Six methods, each looking at the market from a different distance. Tap one to jump there.

interviews.

Seven themes kept coming up, from people who'd been here for fifty years to people worried it won't last ten more. Numbered by how often we heard each one; pick a theme to hear who raised it.

personas.

Five people who depend on the market, inside it and around it. Tap one to find them on the stakeholder map.

stakeholders.

Some stakeholders are in the market every day. Others shape it from the outside and rarely set foot in it.

a day in the life.

Valiben runs a roadside toy stall. The stall opens at 5pm, but her day starts at 6am. Drag around the clock, or tap a slice.

homesourcingrestgetting therethe stall

Naresh and Vani have sold leather belts on the C.G. Road pavement for over 30 years. We followed one evening, from deciding when to leave home to packing up.

Circle size shows how much of the evening each part takes.

Five vendors ranked the market's five biggest problems. The louder the line, the higher it ranked. Pick a vendor to see their order.

5 of 5 vendors put the washrooms first. Parking ranked low because it mostly bothers shoppers on busy days.

tourists

4 of 5 vendors named passers-by as their main customers. The market runs on impulse more than loyalty.

the zine.

A market this layered needed an outcome that felt just as raw and personal, so we made a zine. It carries the market's voices, routines and quiet negotiations, and it was built to be felt as well as read.

Speculative FictionWorld Building

Specimen001

Specimen001 imagines a future where centuries of industrial breeding and genetic manipulation trigger a global mutation, shrinking all cattle into pocket-sized beings.

Overview

Specimen001 imagines a future where centuries of industrial breeding and genetic manipulation trigger a global mutation, shrinking all cattle into pocket-sized beings. With cows no longer viable for milk or meat production, the last original-sized cow is cryogenically preserved while its final batch of milk becomes one of the world’s most valuable commodities.

Through speculative artifacts including tickets, postcards, and institutional documents, the project examines how scarcity transforms everyday resources into symbols of power, luxury, and cultural memory.

Context

Modern cattle are among the most heavily engineered animals on Earth. Through selective breeding, artificial insemination, and industrial farming, humans have continuously reshaped their bodies to maximize milk and meat production. Specimen001 extends this trajectory into a plausible speculative future, asking what might happen if prolonged human intervention resulted in an irreversible biological response.

Themes Explored
  • Industrial Food Systems
  • Animal Exploitation
  • Genetic Mutation
  • Food Inequality
  • Ecological Loss
  • Commodification of Nature
  • Preservation Politics
  • Conservation Futures
The World

In this future, cows no longer occupy fields but display cases. Once valued for their productivity, they are now protected for their rarity. Natural milk has become a luxury reserved for the wealthy, while synthetic substitutes sustain the global population. The last original-sized cow exists as both scientific infrastructure and cultural icon, preserved indefinitely as society attempts to safeguard what it spent centuries reshaping.

Artifact Gallery

Artifact 01 — Ticket Series

Entry tickets for the fictional Bovine Preservation Facility, showing how preservation becomes a paid public spectacle.

Artifact 02 — Postcard Card

A postcard from the fictional preservation facility, combining visitor-world branding with a scale comparison of original-sized cattle and miniature cows. It turns the last cow into cultural memory, tourism, and institutional evidence.

Case File — Specimen001

The artifacts on this page are fragments from a larger speculative fiction. Read the full archive to enter the world of Specimen001, from the mutation of cattle populations to the final milking ceremony and the preservation of the last original-sized cow.
